issues.legal_issue: An allottee who remains in government accommodation after the permitted retention period is liable for market-rate damages even if no notice of that liability was served.
material_facts: The officer was transferred away from the place where his government flat was allotted and was entitled to retain it only for a concessional period of two months.
The allotment rules, which the officer had agreed to follow, deemed the allotment cancelled after that period.
The officer remained in the flat for nearly five years after the permitted period, and the government later claimed market-rate damages.
issues.conclusion: Liability to pay damages equal to the market rate for unauthorised occupation was absolute and did not depend on the Directorate of Estates first serving notice of that liability.
issues.legal_principle: Under SR 317-B-11(2) and (3), an allotment may be retained only for the permitted period and is then deemed cancelled; under SR 317-B-22, an officer who remains in occupation after cancellation is liable for damages equal to the market licence fee. The liability is not contingent on prior notice. Section 7(2) of the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971, and Rule 8(c) of the 1971 Rules provide for recovery and assessment of damages for unauthorised occupation.

predicates.government_accommodation_retention_case: The case concerns a person retaining government accommodation allotted to that person.
predicates.allotment_ended_after_permitted_period: The allotment ended when the permitted retention period expired.
predicates.occupant_remained_in_accommodation: The former allottee continued to occupy the accommodation after the allotment ended.

issues.definition: When an allotment has ended after the permitted retention period and the former allottee remains in the accommodation, the former allottee is liable for market-rate damages.

issues.legal_issue: Government inaction in collecting market-rate damages does not establish that the government relaxed the applicable accommodation rules.
material_facts: The officer remained in government accommodation after his allotment had been cancelled.
The government continued charging normal rent and did not collect market-rate damages during the period of unauthorised occupation.
There was no specific government order relaxing the rules for the officer, with reasons recorded in writing.
issues.conclusion: The government’s failure to collect market-rate rent did not support a presumption that it had relaxed the rules in the officer’s favour.
issues.legal_principle: SR 317-B-25 permits relaxation of the rules in a case of an officer, residence, class of officers, or type of residence only for reasons recorded in writing. Relaxation therefore requires a specific order; it cannot be presumed from government inaction or non-collection of rent.

predicates.government_accommodation_retention_case: The case concerns a person retaining government accommodation allotted to that person.
predicates.government_did_not_collect_market_rate: The government did not collect market-rate charges while the person remained in the accommodation.
predicates.no_written_relaxation_order: The government made no specific written order recording reasons for relaxing the applicable rules.

issues.definition: When the government does not collect market-rate charges but makes no specific written relaxation order, its inaction does not establish that it relaxed the applicable rules.

issues.legal_issue: Promissory estoppel does not prevent the government from claiming damages for unauthorised occupation where it made no inducing representation and the occupant did not change position in reliance on one.
material_facts: The officer had declared that his allotment was subject to the applicable rules and did not notify the authorities of his transfer.
The officer continued occupying the flat and paid normal rent, but the government did not represent that he could remain there on that basis.
There was no evidence that the officer changed his position to his detriment in reliance on any government representation.
issues.conclusion: Promissory estoppel did not prevent the government from claiming market-rate damages for the period of unauthorised occupation.
issues.legal_principle: Estoppel requires a representation of existing fact, belief and action by the other party on the faith of that representation, and resulting detriment. The Court found no representation or conduct intended to induce the officer to believe he could remain in the accommodation on payment of normal rent, and no detrimental change of position in reliance on the government.

predicates.government_accommodation_retention_case: The case concerns a person retaining government accommodation allotted to that person.
predicates.government_made_no_inducing_representati: The government made no representation intended to lead the occupant to believe that continued occupation was permitted on the terms claimed.
predicates.occupant_did_not_change_position_in_reli: The occupant did not change position to the occupant’s detriment in reliance on a government representation.

issues.definition: If the government made no inducing representation and the occupant did not change position to the occupant’s detriment in reliance on one, promissory estoppel does not apply.

issues.legal_issue: The government may not unilaterally deduct a debt from unpaid commuted pension protected from seizure, although it may pursue an authorised recovery process or a suit.
material_facts: The government reduced the damages demand on compassionate grounds and deducted the resulting amount from the officer’s commuted pension before it had been paid to him.
The deduction was made unilaterally, and the officer challenged it as contrary to the protection given to pension money.
The Court held that the government could instead pursue recovery through proceedings under the public-premises legislation or by a suit.
issues.conclusion: The government had no authority to deduct the amount unilaterally from the commuted pension and was required to refund it, without prejudice to pursuing recovery through the available legal procedures.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Pensions Act, 1871 protects pension and money due or to become due on account of pension from seizure, attachment, or sequestration. The Court held that this language includes commuted pension that remains unpaid. It followed Union of India v. Jyoti Chit Fund & Finance, which held that protected pension amounts retain their character until they reach the employee. The Court also considered Crowe v. Price, Municipal Council, Salem v. B. Gururaja Rao, C. Gopalachariar v. Deep Chand Sowcar, and Hassomal Sangumal v. Diaromal Laloomal. It left the government at liberty to pursue recovery under section 7(2) read with section 14 of the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971, or by suit.

predicates.government_debt_recovery_from_pension_ca: The government sought to recover a debt from money payable to a pensioner.
predicates.pension_money_remained_unpaid: The pension money had not yet been paid to or received by the pensioner.
predicates.government_deducted_amount_unilaterally: The government deducted the amount without pursuing an authorised recovery process or obtaining a court order.

issues.definition: When the government seeks to recover a debt from unpaid pension money by unilateral deduction, that deduction is prohibited.
